newsitem.title: ITALY: U.S. envoy welcomes Burundi negotiations.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy welcomes Burundi negotiations.

text.p: U.S. envoy Howard Wolpe on Thursday welcomed direct talks between Burundi's government and the main Hutu rebel group and said forces in the country who sought to disrupt the delicate peace process should face condemnation.
"We believe and we are hopeful that the parties are really serious about these efforts," Wolpe, President Bill Clinton's special envoy for Burundi, said.
"We hope that both parties will act in the public arena in ways that will support and sustain these sensitive discussions," he told Reuters in a telephone interview.
More than 150,000 people have died in Burundi since October 1993 when the country's first freely-elected president was murdered by Tutsi troops in an attempted coup.

Burundi's military ruler Pierre Buyoya, who took power in an army coup last July, confirmed for the first time on Tuesday that his government had held direct talks with the Hutu rebel National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD).
He said the talks had taken place in Rome and had made progress towards a ceasefire. Up to now senior officials have denied the contacts, fearing a backlash from extremist Tutsis.
"My government believes that anyone who would seek to interfere with the process should receive the condemnation of the international community," Wolpe said. He declined to elaborate.
Wolpe, a former congressman, was in Rome to meet members of the Sant'Egidio Community, a Roman Catholic peace group, on his way back to Washington from Zaire.
He said Sant'Egidio was acting as the facilitator in the Burundi talks, which he said were "ongoing". Sant'Egidio said it would give details at a news conference on Friday (1000 GMT).

Wolpe said the U.S. government had been "very encouraged" by the Rome talks and what he called a "remarkable international effort" involving South Africa, Belgium and the European Union as well as the United States to sustain the peace effort.
"We commend the president and the leadership of the CNDD for their courage," Wolpe said.
"There will only be lasting peace and stability (in Burundi) when the political issues underlying the conflict are addressed through negotiations.

"This is always the difficulty in Burundi because there has been so much killing and so much death. The levels of fear and mistrust are so great that it has always been difficult to get this process off the ground," Wolpe said.
Regional states made unconditional talks between the government and rebels a condition of lifting sanctions imposed last July after Buyoya's coup. The blockade was eased last month.

Buyoya said on Tuesday that a sovereign "National Conference", to include all parties including rebels based outside the country, would be held as part of a three-stage dialogue. He gave no timetable for the process.
